voiceInstructions: Warm, engaging female teacher with a natural General American English accent. Relaxed, welcoming and lightly playful, with a gentle smile and conversational rhythm. Keep scientific terms precise and avoid an announcer cadence. Slow down for equations, numbers and conversions. Give brief natural thinking pauses after questions. Do not add words or laughter absent from the script.
title: Wave applications: follow the particle, not just the pattern

chapters.title: Three different rates in one wave equation
chapters.formula: y = 0.02 sin(4 pi x - 20 pi t); v_wave = omega/k; v_particle = partial y/partial t
points: Hold phase constant to find propagation direction and speed.
Hold position fixed to find a particle's transverse velocity and acceleration.
The ideal travelling-wave equation is partial_tt y = v_wave^2 partial_xx y.
chapters.script: Hey, welcome back. A crest moves along a rope, but a marked bit of rope oscillates locally. Let's make that difference numerical. In SI units, displacement y is zero point zero two times sine of four pi x minus twenty pi t. Amplitude is two centimetres, wave number is four pi per metre, and angular frequency is twenty pi radians per second. To follow a crest, keep its phase constant. Four pi x minus twenty pi t stays fixed, so x increases at five metres per second. That is the pattern speed, along positive x. Now watch one particle at a fixed position. Differentiate with respect to time while keeping x unchanged. Its transverse velocity is minus zero point four pi times cosine of the phase. At x zero and time zero, the particle is crossing equilibrium downward at about one point two six metres per second. Pause: zero displacement did not mean zero velocity. Its acceleration is minus angular frequency squared times displacement. At that instant acceleration is zero. A quarter period later, the particle is at its negative extreme: velocity is zero and acceleration is upward. There is also a useful equation check. Taking two time derivatives gives minus omega squared times y; taking two position derivatives gives minus k squared times y. Their ratio gives the ideal wave equation: the second time derivative equals pattern speed squared times the second position derivative. This is a linear, nondispersive wave model, not a promise for every real medium. Always ask which rate the problem wants before substituting numbers.

chapters.title: Standing waves have local amplitude and phase
chapters.formula: y = 0.04 sin(pi x) cos(100 pi t), 0 <= x <= 2 m; local amplitude = |0.04 sin(pi x)|
points: Nodes have zero amplitude, not merely zero instantaneous displacement.
Particles within one loop share temporal phase; neighbouring loops oscillate oppositely.
Each constituent travelling wave has amplitude 0.02 m; antinodes reach 0.04 m.
chapters.script: Now the pattern stands still. A two metre string fixed at both ends has displacement zero point zero four times sine of pi x times cosine of one hundred pi t, again in SI units. The position factor sets each particle's amplitude. The time factor sets its oscillation. Nodes occur where sine of pi x is zero: at zero, one and two metres. There are two loops, so this is the second harmonic, with wavelength two metres and frequency fifty hertz. Each travelling component therefore has speed one hundred metres per second. Notice that a stationary pattern does not mean the particles are stationary. At x equal to one quarter metre, the local amplitude is zero point zero four divided by the square root of two, about two point eight three centimetres. That particle's maximum transverse speed is its local amplitude times one hundred pi, about eight point eight nine metres per second. Why isn't it the antinode value? Because amplitude depends on position. Compare particles at one quarter metre and one and one quarter metres. Their sine factors have opposite signs, so their motions are opposite at the same time: a phase difference of pi. Two points inside the same loop have the same temporal phase, though their amplitudes can differ. At a node phase of displacement is undefined because the amplitude is zero. Finally, the four centimetre antinode amplitude comes from two equal, opposite travelling waves, each with amplitude two centimetres. Do not assign the full standing-wave amplitude to each component. Those checks prevent several common JEE errors.

chapters.title: Use beats to decide which frequency is higher
chapters.formula: f_beat = |f_unknown - f_reference|; equal-amplitude envelope = 2A |cos(pi delta_f t)|
points: Counting beats alone leaves two possible frequencies.
A known increase or decrease in one frequency resolves the ambiguity.
For unequal amplitudes, the quiet intervals need not be silent.
chapters.script: Let's finish with a detective problem. A reference tuning fork is two hundred and fifty six hertz. Another fork produces four beats per second with it. What is the unknown frequency? Think before choosing. It could be two hundred and fifty two or two hundred and sixty hertz. An absolute difference does not tell us which is higher. Now the question states that adding a small load lowers the unknown fork's frequency, and the beats decrease from four to three per second. If the original frequency were two hundred and fifty two, lowering it would move it farther from the reference and increase the beats. That contradicts the observation. So the original frequency was two hundred and sixty hertz; after the change it is two hundred and fifty nine, assuming the stated small change stays on the same side of the reference. The direction of the change matters as much as the beat count. Why is beat frequency the full frequency difference, not half? Adding two equal-amplitude nearby tones produces a rapid carrier multiplied by a slowly changing cosine envelope. That signed cosine changes sign, but loudness depends on its magnitude or its square. Two adjacent loud maxima occur one divided by the frequency difference seconds apart. For a four hertz difference, they are a quarter second apart. With unequal amplitudes, the minimum amplitude is the absolute difference of the two amplitudes, so quiet moments need not be silence. This elementary beat model assumes stable nearby frequencies and comparable amplitudes. Our routine is simple: identify the measured quantity, preserve both initial possibilities, then use the physical change to decide.

quiz.question: For y = 0.02 sin(4 pi x - 20 pi t) in SI units, pattern velocity is:
quiz.explanation: Constant phase gives x = 5t + constant, hence +5 m/s.

quiz.question: For that wave, transverse particle velocity at x = 0, t = 0 is:
quiz.explanation: Partial differentiation at fixed x gives -0.4 pi cos(phase); at phase zero this is -0.4 pi m/s.

quiz.question: For y = 0.04 sin(pi x) cos(100 pi t) on a fixed 2 m string, the number of loops is:
quiz.explanation: Nodes are x = 0, 1 and 2 m, making two loops and the second harmonic.

quiz.question: For that standing wave, points x = 0.25 m and x = 1.25 m oscillate:
quiz.explanation: Their sine position factors have opposite signs; temporal phase differs by pi.

quiz.question: A 256 Hz reference gives 4 beats/s with an unknown fork. A small decrease of the unknown frequency reduces beats to 3/s without crossing the reference. Its original frequency is:
quiz.explanation: Lowering a 260 Hz fork moves it toward 256; lowering a 252 Hz fork moves it away. Original frequency is 260 Hz.
